messages.content:
Proposition:  In 1 Corinthians 7:10-15, Paul says Jesus’ teachings on marriage, 
divorce, and remarriage in the Gospels only apply to marriages between two 
Christians.  
1 Corinthians 7 Context: - The Corinthians loved to import ideas from the Greco-Roman culture around them 
into the church.  Here the idea was that a celibate lifestyle was more holy. - They were influenced by Greek dualism which viewed our material bodies as evil 
and our souls as good.  This false idea led to two extremes for the Corinthians:  - 1) It doesn’t matter what we do with our bodies.  Our flesh is evil, we have 
evil appetites, and to fulfill those evil appetites is just like filling our stomach’s 
appetite with food.  This led to their sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6:12-20 
and Paul had to tell them their bodies are holy temples to God and must NEVER 
be used for evil, especially not joining them to a prostitute. - 2) Our bodies should be deprived of all pleasure, even sex with one’s 
spouse, because if it feels good to the body, it must be evil.  This is likely the 
background for 1 Corinthians 7.  Some of them believed a celibate lifestyle was 
the holier way to live.  They apparently wrote a letter to him in which they argued 
“It is good for a man not to touch a woman (sexually)” (7:1).  Which led to one of 
four outcomes: - A) Either one or both spouses in marriages would refuse to have sex with 
their spouse.  So in 1 Corinthians 7:1-5, Paul has to tell married couples to 
“stop depriving one another” (v. 5) and that husbands and wives have a duty 
to meet each other’s sexual needs.  - B) Those who are single may decide never to get married.  Paul 
recognizes in 1 Corinthians 7:6-9 not everyone has his gift of being able to 
stay single without burning with passion.  He knows if married couples start 
depriving one another of sex, or if unmarried people refuse to ever get 
married, Satan might tempt them because of their lack of self-control (v. 5b). - C) One or both Christian spouses in a marriage would decide it’s better 
to get a divorce and live single.  This is what Paul addresses in 1 
Corinthians 7:10-11.  Christians would want to live holy lives to please the 
Lord, and if they believe a celibate life is more pleasing to God, then either 
one or both of them would be motivated to get a divorce.  So Paul instructs 
them in 7:10-11 not to get divorced at all, and if someone does divorce their 
spouse, they must either stay single or be reconciled to the spouse they 
divorced.  - Note:  The term “leave” or “separate” in v. 10 in a Greco-Roman context 
was divorce, not what we would call “separation.”  All you had to do in 
Greco-Roman society to divorce your spouse is leave.  You didn’t need any 
legal documentation at all; if you’re the woman you usually didn’t own the 
home, so you’d just pack up your stuff and leave.  If you’re the husband, 
1
you can send your wife packing.  Paul’s saying, “DO NOT do this!  Marriage 
is for life!” - Key:  When Paul says, “Not I, but the Lord,” in v. 10, he’s reminding them of 
what Jesus taught on marriage, divorce, and remarriage in Matthew 
5:31-32, 19:3-9, Mark 10:10-12, and Luke 16:18. - Now, Jesus did not explicitly use the words from 1 Corinthians 7:11, “If 
she does leave, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled,” but it was 
implied in Jesus’ teaching.  Jesus said if someone divorces their spouse 
for reasons other than sexual immorality and marries another, it’s 
adultery.  Likewise, if someone marries a person who had been previously 
divorced for reasons other than sexual immorality, it’s adultery.  So the 
logical implication is, if either one of the partners considering remarriage 
participated in a divorce for reasons other than sexual immorality, they 
can’t get remarried.  They would have to either stay unmarried or be 
reconciled to the spouse who divorced them. - So in 1 Corinthians 7:10-11, there are no new teachings at all.  This is 
just a review of what Jesus taught on the subject. - D) A Christian spouse married to a non-Christian spouse would decide 
it’s better to get a divorce and live single.  In addition to believing it’s holier 
to live a celibate lifestyle, this would add another layer of motivation for the 
Christian to divorce their spouse.  Because not only is it unholy and evil to 
have sex, but maybe because their spouse isn’t a Christian the whole marital 
union is unholy to God!  And maybe even their children are unclean and 
defiled!  This is what Paul addresses in 1 Corinthians 7:12-15.- He tells the Christian spouse NOT to divorce their non-Christian spouse, 
BUT in the event that the unbelieving spouse is the one who leaves, he says 
the Christian spouse “is not under bondage in such cases, but God has 
called us to peace.” (v. 15). - I’ll make a case for this below, but I believe the most natural reading of 
“not under bondage,” means “not under bondage to the marriage,” and 
by implication, “not under bondage to remain unmarried or be 
reconciled” like the Christian spouses were in v. 11.  
Key:  When Paul says in v. 12, “To the rest I say, not the Lord,” he is saying Jesus’ 
teachings on marriage, divorce, and remarriage in the Gospels (and reiterated in 1 
Corinthians 7:10-11) only applied to Christians.  Paul is saying that Jesus never 
addressed divorces between Christians and non-Christians, so he’s addressing it now.  
What else could, “I say, not the Lord” mean? - Option 1:  This is uninspired advice.  Paul’s saying, “I’m personally teaching this, but 
this isn’t from Jesus.” - Problem:  Paul was clear when he was just giving his own opinion, like in 1 
Corinthians 7:6 where he says, “This isn’t a command (for married couples to 
pause sex for a period of prayer in v. 5)” or in v. 26, where he says, “I think this is 
2
good in view of the present distress, that it is good for a man to remain as he is.”  
We know that’s not a command, because two verses later in v. 28 he says, “But if 
you marry, you have not sinned…I’m just trying to spare you.”  Paul believed it was 
better to stay single because of hard times coming their way (“the present 
distress”), but he wasn’t commanding them to do so, especially because he 
knows “it’s better to marry than to burn with passion” (v. 9). - But in v. 12-15 there’s no indication that Paul is okay with the Corinthians 
disobeying what he’s saying here, and unless we’re given some clear reason to 
believe these teachings are optional, the rule in 1 Corinthians 14:37 applies 
here:  “The things which I write to you are the Lord’s commandment.”  - Option 2:  Paul’s not saying Jesus’ teachings on MDR don’t apply to non-Christians.  
He’s just saying this specific scenario of a Christian and non-Christian being married 
wasn’t something Jesus addressed, and Paul is now applying Jesus’ teachings to 
their situation too. - Problem #1:  There were other things Jesus never addressed during His ministry 
that Paul addressed in 1 Corinthians, like Christians dividing into factions based 
on who baptized them (1 Corinthians 1), the difference between planters and 
waterers (1 Corinthians 3), Christians taking each other to court (1 Corinthians 6), 
eating meat sacrificed to idols (1 Corinthians 8-10), etc.  Yet Paul never felt the 
need to say, “I say, not the Lord,” for any of those other issues.  So why only say 
that right before the teachings on marriage and divorce between a Christian and a 
non-Christian?- Problem #2:  Paul gives a different instruction in the case of a divorce in v. 15 than 
he does in v. 11.  If Jesus’ teachings in v. 11 applied to mixed marriages between 
Christians and non-Christians too, Paul could have just said that.  But instead he 
gives a different instruction in case of a divorce in v. 15 than he did in v. 11. - To be clear, he gives the SAME instruction to Christians in mixed marriages that 
he gave to Christians married to Christians in v. 10 — DON’T divorce your 
spouse!  That teaching from Jesus applied to Christians married to Christians 
AND to a Christian married to a non-Christian.  Christians are commanded not 
to divorce, whether married to a Christian or not. - The difference is that in v. 11 if a Christian spouse leaves (presumably for 
reasons other than sexual immorality as per Jesus’ teachings in the Gospels), 
they must remain unmarried or be reconciled, and so must the Christian 
spouse they divorced!  - But if a non-Christian spouse leaves in v. 15, the Christian spouse is NOT 
under bondage to that marriage anymore, which means they no longer have 
any obligation to remain unmarried or be reconciled!  That marriage is over 
when the non-Christian spouse leaves and there’s no remaining obligation for 
the Christian to stay unmarried or be reconciled.  They are not under bondage 
to that marriage in any way — they are free. - Note:  I realize I’m assuming “not under bondage” means “not under 
bondage to the marriage,” even though I haven’t proved that yet.  I plan to 
prove it below, but even if you hold a different view on “not under 
bondage,” it cannot be denied that Paul never says in v. 15 that the 
3
Christian is to remain single or be reconciled.  At best, you have to assume 
that what he said back in v. 11 still applies in v. 15, but he doesn’t say that.  
He seems to be giving a DIFFERENT instruction in case of a non-Christian 
divorce than he did back in v. 11 for a Christian divorce. - Option 3:  What makes the most sense is for “I say, not the Lord,” to mean Jesus 
never addressed mixed marriages between Christians and non-Christians during His 
ministry, and by logical extension, He never addressed marriages between two non
Christians either.  His teachings in Matthew 5, 19, Mark 10, and Luke 16 only applied to 
marriages between two Christians. 
And now, through the apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 7, Jesus is addressing 
marriages between Christians and non-Christians and is saying the consequence for a 
non-Christian divorcing a Christian is different from a Christian divorcing a Christian.
What else could “Not under bondage” mean? - Before asking what “not under bondage” means, it’s important to ask, “In what 
sense was the Christian in bondage before the non-Christian divorced them?”  
Whatever bondage the Christian would be freed from if the non-Christian left is the 
bondage the Christian would still be under if the non-Christian stayed.  - Option 1:  Under bondage to convert their spouse. - When Paul says in v. 16, “How do you know whether you will save your husband or 
wife?” maybe the Christian spouse thought they were obligated — or under 
bondage — to convert their non-Christian spouse.  They may have thought, “I 
have to either divorce them or convert them so our marital union and children can 
be holy (v. 14).” - Problems:  - A) Paul says “you’re not under bondage in such cases.”  He clearly means “in 
such cases in which the non-Christian spouse divorces the Christian spouse.”  
Which would imply there are cases in which the non-Christian spouse stays 
and the Christian spouse IS under bondage to convert their non-Christian 
spouse.  That doesn’t match with what we know of the rest of Scripture.  No 
Christian is ever under bondage to convert anyone.   - B) Even if we soften it and say, “Maybe the Corinthians didn’t feel bound to 
convert them, but at least to evangelize to them,” it seems odd for Paul to 
say, “Once they divorce you, you’re not under bondage to try to teach them 
about Jesus anymore.” - v. 16 is just an added note of reassurance, because if a non-Christian 		
spouse divorces their Christian spouse, the Christian spouse may be 		
devastated not just at the loss of relationship, but they may lose all peace 
thinking it’s hopeless for their spouse to ever come to Christ now. - So Paul assures them that even if the non-Christian spouse stayed in 		
the marriage, it wouldn’t be a guarantee of their conversion. - Option 2:  Under bondage to stay married to the non-Christian at all costs. 
4
- Certainly the Christian spouse would feel a sense of obligation to keep their 
marriage together.  They know how serious marriage is according to Jesus’ 
teachings and would want to do what they could to keep it together.  So if the 
non-Christian divorces them, the Christian spouse might feel like they failed God 
in some way because it was their duty to keep the marriage together.  This is 
based on the phrase “let him leave” in 1 Corinthians 7:15.  Perhaps the Christian 
spouse was unwilling to let the non-Christian spouse divorce them.- In this option, Paul is assuring them they’re not under bondage to keep the 
marriage together or make the non-Christian stay.  It takes two to tango, and 
even if a Christian does everything in their power to keep the marriage together, 
the non-Christian’s decision to leave is not in the Christian’s control. - Problems:  - A) This scenario isn’t fair to the context.  It doesn’t seem like Corinthian 
Christians were struggling because they desperately were trying to make sure 
their non-Christian spouses stayed.  No, the opposite was true.  The Christian 
spouse was wondering if THEY should be the ones to divorce their non
Christian spouse! - That’s why Paul starts the discussion in 1 Corinthians 7:12 by commanding 
the Christian spouse not to divorce the non-Christian spouse. - If Christian spouses in Corinth believed they were truly under bondage to 
stay married to a non-Christian, it seems odd they were the ones thinking 
about leaving. - B) Why would anyone in their day, even Christians, have thought they were 
under bondage to keep the other spouse from leaving?  There’s no teaching 
anywhere in Scripture that gives any indication a husband or wife is under 
bondage to force their spouse not to divorce them.  Certainly we should do 
everything in our power to preserve the marriage, but God gave us all free will.  - When God divorced Israel for their sin of idolatry in Jeremiah 3:6-8, 
certainly God did everything He could to reason with His “wife,” but He was 
never under bondage to keep Israel from leaving Him. - C) Paul already acknowledged that whether or not the non-Christian spouse 
leaves is fully dependent on their own consent — their own free will choice — 
in 7:12-13.  Whether or not they stay has nothing to do with whether the 
Christian spouse can force them to stay, but whether the non-Christian 
“consents to live” with them.  - D) Paul says “you’re not under bondage in such cases.”  Which would mean 
IF the non-Christian spouse leaves, the Christian spouse is not under 
bondage to make them stay.  But if the non-Christian spouse stays, then the 
Christian spouse IS under bondage to make them stay?  Again, that doesn’t 
make sense because no one is under bondage to make sure their spouse 
doesn’t divorce them. 
Option 3:  Not under bondage to renounce Christ to keep the marriage together.- This option envisions a scenario where the non-Christian spouse issues an 		
ultimatum to their Christian spouse:  “Either renounce your faith in Christ or I’m 		
5
	leaving you!”  Maybe they were both non-Christians when they got married, then 
	one becomes a Christian and the non-Christian isn’t happy about it!
		- So Paul is assuring the Christian spouse they’re not under bondage to 		
		renounce Jesus to keep their non-Christian spouse from leaving. 
 		- Problems:  - A) There’s nothing in the context that indicates this is what was 		
			happening.  Again, the main issue in context was Christian 			
			spouses wanting to leave their non-Christian spouses, not the 		
			other way around. 
			- B) Paul never says why the non-Christian spouse wants to leave, 		
			so it’s a huge assumption to think they’re leaving simply because 		
			their spouse is a Christian.  Unbelievers got divorces all the time 		
			for all kinds of reasons, and Paul gives no indication that he’s 		
			limiting it to a difference in faith here. 
			- C) Jesus was already very clear He came to bring a sword and 		
			divide households against each other, and that we must love Him 		
			even MORE than our own family members.  So why would any 		
			Christian think they were under bondage to choose their spouse 		
			over Jesus?  Especially since Jesus says there won’t even be 		
			marriage in Heaven! (Matthew 22:30)
			- D) Paul says “you’re not under bondage in such cases.”  Which 		
			would mean IF the non-Christian spouse leaves, the Christian 		
			spouse is not under bondage to renounce Christ to make them 		
			stay.  But if the non-Christian spouse stays, then the Christian 		
			spouse IS under bondage to renounce Christ to make them stay?  		
			That doesn’t make sense.
Option 4:  Not under bondage to remain in the condition in which you were called. 
	- This is the view I’ve held for at least the past decade.  In the Greco-Roman 		
	world, social 	status was everything.  It was all about gaining honor and avoiding 		
	shame, and one of the ways you gained status in society was based on your 		
	social position.  Your social position was connected to who your family was, 		
	what kind of job you had, how much money you had, and whether you had 		
	social relationships with people of high status. 
		- Well, it seems like they were importing that idea into the church, 			
		thinking if they want to have a higher status to GOD and be viewed more 		
		honorably by Him, they need to change their social position in life. 
			- So if they’re married, they’re thinking they need to change that 		
			social status to single to be more approved by God because the 		
			celibate lifestyle is holier.  This is ESPECIALLY true if they’re 			
			married to a non-Christian because in their culture it was absurd to 
			marry someone of lower status than you because that lowers your 		
			status as a result.  So to get their status back, they might think 		
			they need to divorce their lower status non-Christian spouse.  If 		
			they’re a slave, they think they need to be free in order to gain 		
			more status in God’s eyes.  If they’re Jewish and have been 			
6
			circumcised, they’re thinking they need to be more sophisticated 		
			like the Greeks and become uncircumcised (yes somehow they 		
			could do this back then).  If they’re Greeks, they may think they 		
			need to get circumcised to be holier like the Jews. 
 - So there’s this whole social upheaval going on because they think they have to 
change things about their social life in order to improve their status in the church and 
with God. 
	- And Paul addresses this most directly in 1 Corinthians 7:17-24 and makes it 		
	clear NONE of that is necessary!  In summary, he says in 7:20 and 7:24:  			
	“Each man must remain in that condition in which he was called.” 
	- So then in 1 Corinthians 7:15 when Paul says, “You're not under bondage if 		
	your non-Christian spouse divorces you,” he could be saying, “You’re not under 		
	bondage to stay in the condition in which you were called.  I want you to remain 		
	in the condition in which you’re called, which means to stay married, but if 		
	you’re non-christian spouse leaves you, then you’re obviously not under 			
	bondage to stay in that married condition.” 
	- Problems:   - A) What Paul repeats in v. 20 and 24 is not a command.  If it were a 		
		command, it would make sense that Christians would be “under 			
		bondage” to keep it.  
			- But in v. 21 he says, “Were you called while a slave?  Do not 		
			worry about it; but if you are able to also become free, rather do 		
			that.”  
				- Paul does not say, “If you became a Christian while a 		
				slave, you MUST remain a slave and never change your 		
				condition!”  No he says, “If you can become free, great!  If 		
				you can’t, that’s fine because you can remain in the 			
				condition in which you’re called and still be right with God.  		
				But you’re not required to stay a slave either.”
			- In v. 25-26 he explicitly says this is NOT a command.  It’s just 		
			wise advice in light of the “present distress.” (Perhaps a time of 		
			persecution and hardship)
				- 1 Corinthians 7:25-26 - “I have no command of the Lord, 		
				but I give an opinion…I think this is good in view of the 		
				present distress that it is good for a man to remain as he is.” 
				- Paul is clear, the “command” to remain in the condition in 		
				which you were called from v. 20 and v. 24 is NOT a			
				command.
					- He further demonstrates it in v. 27-28 where he 		
					tells people who are unmarried not to change their 		
					condition by getting married.  Then says, “But if you 		
					do marry, you haven’t sinned.” 
					- Point:  How could “not under bondage” in 7:15 		
					mean “not under bondage to remain in the condition 		
7
in which you were called” if NO ONE is under 			
bondage to do that in this chapter? - B) Paul says “you’re not under bondage in such cases.”  Which 			
would mean IF the non-Christian spouse leaves, the Christian 			
spouse is not under bondage to remain in the condition in which they 		
were called, that is not under bondage to stay married.  But if the non-		
Christian spouse stays, then the Christian spouse IS under bondage to 		
remain in the condition in which they were called and stay married?  		
Basically Paul would be saying, “You’re required to stay married as long 		
as your non-Christian spouse stays with you, but if they divorce you, 		
you’re not required to say married.”   Who would think they were required 		
to stay married after their non-Christian spouse ended the marriage?  		
That doesn’t make sense.- Option 5:  Under bondage to feelings of guilt for what might happen to the souls of 
their non-Christian spouses if they leave.  - If their non-Christian spouse divorces them, the Christian spouse may be feeling 
guilty for not being able to convert them.  This is why after Paul says, they’re “not 
under bondage,” he says, “but God has called us to peace (as opposed to feeling 
guilty).”  Then in v. 16 he asks “How do you know if you’d be able to save them 
anyway if they stayed?” - This view sounds really good on the surface because it does seem like Paul is 
addressing some level of guilt in v. 16, and possibly in v. 15c - “God has called 
us to peace.”- Problems:  - A) The Greek word for “not under bondage” (douloo) is way too strong for 
feelings.  Paul has other vocabulary for guilt, and this word is never used for 
inner emotions.  This is more of an objective bondage — a duty — rather than 
a subjective bondage — a feeling. - B) Just because Paul addresses guilt in v. 15c and v. 16 doesn’t mean “not 
under bondage” means “not under bondage to feel guilt.”  I’m willing to grant 
that some in Corinth may have felt guilty if their non-Christian spouse left 
them, and Paul is comforting them by telling them “God has called us to 
peace, and you don’t know whether you would have saved them anyway.”  
But this doesn’t mean the bondage refers to guilt.  He could very well be 
referring to the marriage bond (option 6 below) and how they aren’t under 
bondage to the marriage anymore, and THEN he addresses any guilt they 
may feel about it afterwards by saying “God has called us to peace and you 
don’t know whether you would have saved them anyway.”
Option 6:  Not under bondage to the marriage - This seems to be the most natural reading of the text. - A) It makes sense of Paul saying, “not under bondage in such cases.”  		
Which means, “In cases where the non-Christian spouse leaves, the 		
Christian spouse is not still under bondage to the marriage.  In cases 		
where 	the non-Christian spouse stays, the Christian spouse IS under 		
8
		bondage to the marriage.”  This is the only view that makes sense of 		
		HOW a Christian spouse is ever under bondage to a non-Christian 			
		spouse.  
			- As covered above, they are not under bondage to Options 1-5 if 		
			the non-Christian spouse stays, but they ARE under bondage to 		
			the marriage if they stay. 
		- B) It fits with the other ways Paul uses bondage to describe marriage in 		
		this chapter. 
			- v. 4-5 - Paul sees married couples as belonging to each other, 		
			almost like they’re under bondage not to deprive one another 		
			sexually because it’s part of their marital duties. 
			- v. 27 - Paul speaks of married life vs. single-hood as being 		
			“bound” vs. being “released.” 
			- v. 32-33 - Paul describes single-hood as being “free from 			
			concern.”  Whereas married couples are not free in the same way.  		
			The implication is that they are bound to each other and are 			
			“concerned” about how to please their spouse, and not just how to 
			please the Lord. 
			- v. 39 - Paul says a wife is “bound” to her husband as long as he 		
			lives.  But if her husband dies, she is “free” to remarry.
				- There’s a contrast in these verses between being bound to 
				a marriage and being free from a marriage.  So in v. 15 when 
				Paul says, “not under bondage,” it makes the most sense 		
				that he’s describing someone free from the bond of 			
				marriage, no longer bound to their spouse. 
		- C) It makes sense of the contrast with Christian marriages in 1 			
		Corinthians 7:10-11. 
			- In the case of a Christian who divorces their Christian spouse, he 		
			or she “must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her 			
			husband.”  Paul is saying they’re still under bondage to this 			
			marriage in some way.  It’s not that they’re still “married in God’s 		
			eyes,” Paul says they are “unmarried.” (I’ll go into detail on 			
			this in part 3 of this study).  But there’s still some obligation they 		
			have to the spouse they divorced not to get remarried, which is 		
			consistent with Jesus who said if they get remarried, it’s 			
			considered adultery.
				- But if a non-Christian divorces a Christian, it’s very natural 		
				to read this as a contrast to 7:10-11 — the Christian is 		
				NOT obligated to stay single or be reconciled because they 		
				are no longer bound to this marriage in any way.
		- D) What else would ever bind a Christian to a non-Christian but a 			
		marriage bond?
			- There’s nothing else in the WORLD that would bind a Christian to 		
			live with a non-Christian (7:12) other than a marriage bond.  It’s the 
			main subject under consideration.  Paul is saying a Christian is 		
			BOUND to the non-Christian and therefore he or she MUST NOT 		
9
			divorce their non-Christian spouse.  As Christians, they have an 		
			obligation and are under bondage to their non-Christian spouse 		
			because they’re married!  BUT in such cases where the non-			
			Christian spouse divorces them, the Christian is no longer under 		
			bondage.  What other thing could Paul be talking about but 			
			marriage that makes sense here?  What other thing is the Christian 
			under bondage to if the non-Christian stays, but not under 			
			bondage to if the non-Christian leaves?  Options 1-5 don’t fit, and I 
			haven’t found any other options that fit either.  Marriage is the only 		
			thing that would bind a Christian to live with a non-Christian. 
	Problems? 
	- The only problem I’ve EVER had with this view is that it contradicts Jesus’ 		
	teaching in Matthew 19:9.  It’s why I’ve never allowed myself to hold this view, 		
	even though it’s the most natural reading in context.  But now that I’ve allowed 		
	myself to accept what Paul said in 1 Corinthians 7:12 that Jesus was NOT 		
	addressing mixed marriages between Christians and non-Christians, I’m finally 		
	free (no pun intended) to accept the most natural view of “not under bondage” in 
	the text.  And I cannot tell you what a RELIEF it is to finally be able to let go of all 
	these other options that have felt so forced and unnatural to me for DECADES 		
	and finally hold a view that makes sense to me and harmonizes perfectly with 		
	what Jesus taught. 
Why does Paul say, “But God has called us in (or to) peace?” in 7:15?  - The meaning of this phrase is determined by which option you take 			
	above.  Whatever it means, it has to match the option you take about the 			
	meaning of “not under bondage”, and truthfully it can match any of the options.  		
	This is why the meaning of this phrase should not DETERMINE which option you 
	take, because it can go with any of them. 
		- Option 1:  If it’s “not under bondage to convert their spouse,” Paul 		
		is saying, “God has called us to peace, not to pressuring or forcing 		
		people into becoming Christians.” 
		- Option 2:  If it’s “not under bondage to keep the marriage together at 		
		all costs,” Paul is saying, “God has called us to peace, not to try to force 		
		someone to stay in a marriage they no longer want to be in.” 
		- Option 3:  If it’s “not under bondage to renounce Christ to keep the 		
		marriage together,” Paul is saying, “God has called us to peace with Him, 		
		not to deny Him and destroy our peace with Him for the sake of saving a 		
		marriage.”

Problems? 
I’ll address 4 main objections to this view below.  But… (is this but and three periods necessary?)
The hardest problem I’ve ever had to address with Option 4 is that it seems 
to contradict Jesus’ teachings in the Gospels.  
If you believe Jesus’ teachings on the consequences of divorce are 
binding on non-Christians too, it would mean if a non-Christian 
divorces a Christian, the Christian and non-Christian are still bound to 
the marriage and therefore must stay single or be reconciled.  
But Paul doesn’t say that.  He says in that case, the Christian is not 
under bondage to the marriage, and the implication is he or she is free 
to remarry — and so is the non-Christian spouse.  In fact, Paul doesn’t 
even attempt to tell the non-Christian to stay single or be reconciled 
because he’s not binding Christ’s teachings about divorce on the non
Christian.  Nor does he tell the Christian spouse to inform the non
Christian spouse about Christ’s teachings on the matter.  Why?  
Because Christ’s teachings about the consequences of divorce don’t 
apply to non-Christians.  Which means both the Christian and the non
Christian would be free from the marriage bond, and therefore free to 
remarry.
This is why I’ve never allowed myself to accept this view, even 
though it’s the strongest view in context.  I think it’s what holds 
most brethren back from accepting too.  But once I realized from 
Paul’s statement, “I, not the Lord,” that Jesus was not addressing 
marriages between Christians and non-Christians (7:12), it 
completely eliminated any supposed contradiction. 
Why does Paul say, “But God has called us in (or to) peace” in 7:15?  
The meaning of this phrase will be determined by which option you take 			
on the meaning of “not under bondage.”  Since it can match any option, the 
meaning of this phrase must not determine which option you take. 
If we choose Option 4, “not under bondage to the marriage,” which is the view 
I’m proposing, this matches in several ways.
1) “God has called us to peace, so whether this non-Christian spouse 		
stays or leaves, we can be at peace with Him.  A Christian’s peace with 		
God is not dependent on what their non-Christian spouse does.”  
2) “God has called us to inner peace, and he doesn’t expect you to feel 		
hopeless about their conversion or guilty for letting them go.”  This 			
second meaning makes good sense of v. 16 where Paul assures them 		
there’s no guarantee they would have been able to convert their spouse 		
anyway. 
10
3) “God has called us to peace with our fellow man, so don’t try to argue 		
with your non-Christian spouse or guilt them into staying when they’re 		
determined to leave.”  
Objections: 
A) “Under Bondage” (douloo in Greek) is too strong a word for marriage.  It means to 
be enslaved to someone, so how could Paul describe the marriage bond with such a 
strong word? 
Answer:  
Paul uses this word to describe making himself a slave to all men in 			
1 Corinthians 9:19, which is a much weaker kind of bondage than marriage.  He 		
also applies it to being enslaved to wine in Titus 2:3, which again is a much 		
weaker bondage than marriage.  The marriage bond is far stronger than these!  
In fact, there is no stronger bond on earth!  God joins us together and 
commands no man to separate us!  So if “bondage” were too strong a word		
for marriage, it would also be too strong for these lesser bonds.
B) The bond Paul mentions in the rest of 1 Corinthians 7 is a different word than the 
one in v. 15.  In 7:15 it’s the word “douloo” but Paul uses the word “deo” to describe 
the marriage bond in 1 Corinthians 7:27 and 39.
1 Corinthians 7:27 - “Are you bound [deo] to a wife?  Do not seek to be 			
released.”  
1 Corinthians 7:39 - “A wife is bound [deo] as long as her husband 				
lives, but if her husband is dead, she is free to be remarry, only in 				
the Lord.”  The Greek word deo is not directly related to slavery, but it’s used to 		
describe being bound by ropes (Mark 3:27), tied up (Mark 11:4), and even 			
imprisoned (Mark 15:7). 
Answers:   
1) It’s perfectly fine to use different words to refer to the same thing.  If I 		
say, “It’s cold outside,” or it’s “chilly outside,” I’m using different words to 		
mean the same thing.  Likewise in 7:15 Paul uses the word “douloo,” 		
which means “to enslave,” and “deo” which means “to bind” in v. 27 and 		
v. 39. 
Clearly these words are in the same family of meaning, and both 		
apply to a lack of freedom.
2) This argument commits what’s called the “exclusive usage” 			
fallacy.  It assumes if a word is never used anywhere else to 				
describe X, it cannot be used in this text to describe X.  The 	argument 		
here is, “Since Paul never used the word “douloo” to describe marriage in 
the rest of the chapter, he cannot mean it to describe marriage in 7:15.”
But Paul has used the term “douloo” in his writings to describe 		
many different kinds of slavery.  Slavery to the Law of Moses (Gal. 	
4:3), slavery to sin (Romans 6:18), slavery to become all things to 		
all men (1 Corinthians 9:19), slavery to the elementary principles of 		
the world (Gal. 4:9).  He seems to use the term loosely in many 
11
different contexts to mean one is bound to an obligation 			
and isn’t free.

contexts, why couldn’t he use the word to apply to a 			
marriage?

remarriage.  Based on the context, the main concern of the Corinthians was 
whether or not they should divorce their spouses, not on whether or not they could 
remarry.  However…
Answer:   
1) Paul brings remarriage up anyway, because it’s directly connected to the 
subject of divorce. (Capitalize V's below)
v. 10-11 - If a Christian spouse divorces their Christian spouse, they are not 
free to remarry.  They must remain unmarried or else be reconciled.
v. 15 - As discussed earlier, “not under bondage” is in contrast to a 
Christian who divorces a Christian and must remain single or be reconciled

divorced by a non-Christian by saying they’re “not under bondage,” which 
implies they do not have to remain single or be reconciled.  They would be 
free to remarry. 
v. 39 - Paul talks about the right of a widow to be remarried after her 
husband dies. 
2) It would seem odd for Paul to mention the non-Christian divorce, then say 
nothing to the Christian about what it means for their future.  I suppose they 
could have just assumed the answer was the same as in 7:11 — that they 
have to stay single or be reconciled — but it makes more sense to see Paul 
preemptively allaying their concerns by assuring them they’re “not under 
bondage in such cases.”   
D) This would mean there’s a teaching of Christ that non-Christians aren’t held 
accountable to, yet Jesus said “All authority has been given to me in Heaven and on 
earth.” 
Answer: 
1) If it doesn’t mean that, (If it doesn't mean what?) we’re forced to explain what Paul means by “I, not the 
Lord.” (7:12).  As I’ve argued above, the strongest explanation is that Jesus’ 
teachings on the consequences of divorce don’t apply to non-Christians.  
2) This led me to ask, “Why would divorce be the one thing Jesus taught that 
doesn’t apply to non-Christians?” 
Then I realized there are a lot more of Jesus’ teachings that don’t apply to 
non-Christians, and it makes perfect sense why they don’t.  In part 2 of 
this study, I’ll explain why this is the case. 
12
But for now, I hope this has been a persuasive attempt to prove my proposal: 
In 1 Corinthians 7:12-15, Paul indicates Jesus’ teachings in the Gospels about 
the consequences of a divorce only apply to Christians, not to non-Christians.
Practical Implications:  
1) Since Jesus did not address marriages between Christians and non-Christians, it 
stands to reason He also did not address marriages between two non-Christians.
It would be VERY odd to say, “Jesus’ teachings on the consequences of 			
divorce apply to marriages between either two Christians or two non-Christians, 
but not to marriages between a Christian and a non-Christian.” 
If that were the case, it would mean if a non-Christian divorced a 			
non-Christian, the non-Christian who was divorced would still be under 
bondage to the marriage.  But if a non-Christian divorced a Christian, the 
Christian who was divorced would not be under bondage to the marriage.  
That doesn’t make sense, because it would hold the non-Christian to a higher 
standard than the Christian.

Christian — even if it was their fault — once they become a Christian they are free 
to remarry.
Why?  Because Christ’s laws on the consequences of divorce in the 			
Gospels did not apply to them when they weren’t Christians. (This is the controversial point)
So whatever happened is in the past now, and they are not required to 		
remain single or be reconciled.

have to divorce their non-Christian spouse.

doesn’t say to the Christians, “Do not divorce your non-Christian spouse unless 		
they’ve been married and divorced in the past, or unless you were married and 		
divorced before becoming a Christian, then you must divorce them.”  No, he 		
just tells them not to get a divorce.  Why?  Because Paul is not applying the 		
consequences of divorce from Jesus’ teachings in the Gospels to non-			
Christians before they became Christians. 
This is why, even though divorce was rampant in the first century, no one 		
in the New Testament was required to get a divorce once they became 			
Christians.  I’ll elaborate more on this in a later study, but…
The Jews and Samaritans believed in divorce for any reason based on 		
Deuteronomy 24.  “Any cause” divorce was the most popular view by far, 		
which is why the Pharisees asked Jesus about this in Matthew 19:3 and 		
why the disciples were so stunned in Matthew 19:10 after learning from 		
Jesus that divorce for any cause is not allowed.  So many Jews and 		
Samaritans were married multiple times and God allowed this under 		
the Law of Moses despite not being ideal.  When Jesus met a 			
13
Samaritan woman in John 4 who had 5 husbands, that wasn’t shocking in 
their day. 
Likewise, Greeks and Romans got divorces all the time for any reason 		
too.  Some of their satirical writers said Roman women marry to get 
divorced, and divorce to get married.  (quotes? and citation?) So in Jesus’ world, you had 
hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of non-Christians with multiple 
marriages and divorces. 
Yet there’s not a single verse anywhere in the New Testament 
and not one shred of evidence from historical sources outside 
the New Testament about them divorcing their spouses upon 
conversion.
Why?  Because they were married and divorced before 			
they became Christians, which means their acts of re-marriage 
were not considered adulterous like they would be for Christians 
because Jesus’ teachings on the consequences of divorce only 
apply to Christians, not to non-Christians.  And that’s what Paul 
indicates in 1 Corinthians 7:12-15.

No, I’m simply saying this view isn’t some newfound doctrine I claim to have
